Scored by the neighbourhoods their children come from, Varndean looked the more deprived school and Longhill the less, so moving Whitehawk looked like evening them out. The published figures put them the other way round, and the second version fitted each school’s pull on disadvantaged children to those figures — but on today’s map. The published figures are whole-school averages for cohorts admitted before the 2024 map and the new priorities, when Whitehawk was in Longhill’s catchment. Fitted on today’s map, Longhill’s pull (1.95) stood in for Whitehawk children it no longer admits, and Varndean’s (0.57) held down the ones it now does; moving Whitehawk then looked like concentrating disadvantage at Longhill. Fitted on the map and rules those cohorts were admitted under, the pulls are 1.47 and 0.80, and the redraw barely moves the index — but that fit still misses what the new rules do. Fitted to the first Year 7 offers under today’s map and priorities, the model’s measure, Longhill’s pull is far stronger, 4.66, because 49% of its September 2026 offers went to children eligible for free school meals; Varndean’s is 0.77. On that measure the redraw raises the index a little, because the model sends Longhill almost only the disadvantaged Whitehawk children: 13 of 13.
How firm that is. As fitted, the redraw changes the index by +0.005; at half the fitted pull by less than a thousandth; with no pull by -0.009. The sign changes with the strength of the pull. The honest reading is that the redraw’s effect on segregation is too small for this model to call. Longhill’s pull rests on a single year of offers at a school that made fewer than a hundred of them on offer day, and it implies that almost every Whitehawk family choosing Longhill would be disadvantaged. A second year of Year 7 offers would test it; the published whole-school figures will not show the 2024 map in full until every year group has been admitted under it, in 2029-30.
What that leaves. The case for or against returning Whitehawk rests on other things: a shorter journey for the children who would take a Longhill place, 11 more children a year for Longhill by 2030, and less displacement. For comparison, the whole pre-2024 map scores 0.118 in 2026, against 0.117 today. And a more or less mixed intake is not the same as better or worse results for the children in it: most of the difference between schools’ headline scores reflects who they teach rather than what they add (Section 2.4).


Priority 6 makes almost no difference. Switched off, the index is 0.117; at 20% it is 0.117 (the priority-6 subsection of section 8). Removing all oversubscription priorities gives 0.110 and displaces 17 children in 2026 against 6.
The power diagram raises segregation on this model — 0.126 — and costs Longhill 12 children. It is not recommended on this evidence.

title: The Brighton Secondary School System
text:
11.4 Priority 3: catchments, journeys and displacement
For parents the first thing is a short journey to a school near home and friends, and the second is not being displaced from it.
Displacement is small and falling. 6 children in 2026 and 2 in 2030 would have taken a place in their catchment and cannot. Options that trim the full schools hard raise it — to 52 in 2026 with Stringer at 270, Varndean at 240 and Blatchington Mill at 270 — and so does removing the priorities. Whitehawk back to Longhill lowers it, to 3 in 2026, because the Whitehawk families who would be refused at a full central school now have a catchment school with room.
The share of children at a school in their own catchment is raised most by the faith schools taking fewer — 61% with Cardinal Newman at 270 and King’s at 150, against 57% — because every child they do not take goes to a catchment school instead, and usually a nearer one: the longest journeys fall to 54 minutes from 55.
Closing Longhill is the option parents would pay most for. It saves the most money — the community schools’ balance is −£0.5m in 2026 against −£1.4m, partly because Longhill’s own deficit leaves the books — but the longest journeys lengthen to 60 minutes, the share travelling over 40 minutes rises to 30%, and more children leave the city: 75 in 2030 against 61. It also lowers segregation more than any other option in the table, to 0.103 against 0.117: Longhill’s Year 7 intake is among the most disadvantaged in the city, and its children would spread across schools with less disadvantaged ones. That is a statistic about intakes, not a benefit to the children who would travel further. It is the counterfactual against which keeping Longhill open is a choice to spend money on shorter journeys in the east.

By 2035 the city carries 720 empty Year 7 places a year, 509 of them in the community schools. Removing them from the community schools alone makes the community schools worse off: their balance goes from −£4.5m to −£5.5m, because the children they no longer have room for go to the academies and faith schools, and 55 are displaced from their catchment. Removing places from every school in proportion does the opposite: −£4.0m, with 5 displaced and 61% of children at a catchment school. A viable system in 2035 is one in which the schools the council does not run shrink with the ones it does, and the council’s case for asking them rests on exactly this comparison.

title: The Brighton Secondary School System
text:
11.6 All three together
Where the priorities agree.

Cardinal Newman and King’s taking fewer helps Priority 1 and Priority 3 together, and the community schools’ finances most of all. It needs the dioceses’ agreement, and the case to put to them is that a city whose cohort is falling cannot keep every school full, and that the schools it does not run are part of the same system.
Reviewing priority 6 touches little. It makes almost no difference to segregation and a small one to displacement, and it gives something real — a route into the popular schools for the children of single-school catchments who use it. The case for keeping it at 5% is as good as the case against.

Where they compete, and which should give.

Whitehawk is not the trade-off it looked. Returning Whitehawk to Longhill’s catchment gives Longhill 11 more children a year by 2030 and lowers displacement, and its effect on how mixed intakes are is small and turns on how disadvantage is counted. It is not the clear trade against segregation earlier versions of this section showed.
Access against segregation. Elm Grove shortens deprived children’s journeys and concentrates them in one school; CoMArt shortens them with little change to how mixed intakes are. If the council values access more, relocation is its strongest tool; if it values mixed intakes more, it should not move Longhill for that reason.
Longhill against short journeys. Trimming the central schools helps Longhill for two or three years and lengthens journeys for the children moved. It should be done only with the Whitehawk redraw, and only while those schools are full.
Money against journeys. Closing Longhill is the cheapest system and the one with the longest journeys in the east. Keeping it open is worth doing only as a deliberate choice to pay for shorter journeys and a school in the east, sized and staffed for the children it will get.


11.6.1 The recommendation

Consider returning Whitehawk to Longhill’s catchment. Returning it to Longhill’s catchment gives Longhill 11 children a year by 2030 and lowers displacement, and gives the children who take a Longhill place a shorter journey. Its effect on how mixed intakes are is small and not reliably in either direction; the case rests on Longhill and on journeys, not on segregation.
Set Longhill’s admission number at 150, and plan its budget and staffing for about a hundred children a year, not for 150. Put the gap between that and break-even — about £0.8m a year on the intake it would have in 2030 with nothing changed — to members as the cost of keeping a school in the east, and decide it as that.
Trim Stringer, Varndean and Blatchington Mill — to 300, 270 and 300 — for the next two or three rounds, while they are full, alongside the redraw, and not without it.
Ask Cardinal Newman to reduce to 300, and King’s to 150, and Brighton Aldridge to 150, and make the case for each school in the city giving up places in proportion by 2030.
Publish where priority 6’s places went, so what it does to segregation can be measured rather than modelled.
Do not move Longhill to raise its roll; consider Elm Grove only as an access decision for deprived children in the east, with the segregation cost stated.

Together — Whitehawk back to Longhill, Longhill at 150, the central trims, priority 6 switched off (the far end of reviewing it), Cardinal Newman at 300 and Brighton Aldridge at 150 — that package gives Longhill 128 children in 2026 and 92 in 2030, against 91 and 75; a segregation index of 0.122 against 0.117; 5 children displaced in 2026 against 6; 58% at a catchment school against 57%; and, in 2026, longest journeys of 53 minutes against 54. It does not make Longhill break even, and it does not shorten deprived children’s journeys. The first needs a decision about money; the second needs a decision about where schools are, or about buses (Section 10.1).






WarningWhat this rests on



Every number here is from a model calibrated to published catchment totals, not to individual applications. The finances are a steady state five years out, with a school shedding three quarters of the cost of a pupil it loses. The catchment terms are carried to redrawn maps at the strength families follow the maps they have, which is what decides every redraw result above. Segregation counts disadvantaged pupils placed by each school’s fitted pull on them, which reproduces the published shares for the cohorts admitted before the 2024 map and priorities, and assumes those pulls hold under today’s rules and when maps and schools change. Most options differ on the index by a few thousandths, which is inside what a change of measure has moved. And the academies and faith schools are modelled as responding to demand, not as making their own decisions about numbers. The direction of each finding is more reliable than its size.
